browserinfo.Title: Browser Information
browserinfo.Note: This page displays two types of browser information: basic information derived from the browser's User Agent, and a browser fingerprint calculated through various data metrics. Browser fingerprints are akin to the fingerprints on your palm; the more information your browser exposes, the higher your uniqueness to websites, making you more easily trackable. Sometimes, even switching to incognito mode or changing browsers may not alter your fingerprint.
browserinfo.Note2: The methods for calculating browser fingerprints are diverse, and different technical approaches may lead to inconsistent results. Here, we use a relatively simple method for calculation.

fingerprint.changeOption: You can try changing the data used to calculate the browser fingerprint to observe variations (remember to compare it in incognito mode).
fingerprint.browserTips: Some browsers, such as Safari, protect users from tracking by generating different fingerprint values each time, even when the same data is selected.

censorshipcheck.Title: Censorship Check
censorshipcheck.Note: Look up where a website has been blocked or interfered with over the past 30 days — and how — based on open data from OONI's global volunteer network. You can then verify suspicious regions with a Globalping realtime probe test. In some countries, internet censorship is clearly defined by law, while in others it is more vague.

censorshipcheck.ResultsHint: Results will appear here after you select probes and run the test.
censorshipcheck.RealtimeNote: You can select multiple probes for real-time connectivity testing to comprehensively evaluate the website's block status. When running the test, 2 probes will be executed per country; matching results from both probes indicate higher reliability.
censorshipcheck.RealtimeFooterNote: Realtime probes mostly run from datacenter networks; their results can differ from actual residential-network observations, as some websites may block access from datacenter networks. Please read them together and make a judgment based on the actual situation.

invisibilitytest.Title: Invisibility Test
invisibilitytest.Note: When you use a proxy or VPN, do the websites you visit really not know that you are using a proxy? Are you truly invisible? We will use various methods to try to calculate the vulnerabilities in your disguise and find evidence that you are using a proxy. Although some test results may not be completely accurate, this test is still highly informative.
invisibilitytest.Note2: After clicking Run, the system will run a script that usually completes all tests within 10 seconds. During this process, your IP information, browser information, etc. will be collected and analyzed in the background.

personacheck.Title: In-depth Persona Check
personacheck.Note: There is an old test: if it looks like a duck, swims like a duck and quacks like a duck, it probably is a duck. Sites read you the same way — your IP may claim you are in country A, but your time zone, languages, installed fonts, keyboard and a dozen other signals each tell their own story, and together they are the persona a site actually sees. This tool measures that persona, compares it against the local resident you want to be read as, and shows exactly where the two diverge.
personacheck.NoteVs: It asks a different question than the Invisibility Test. That one checks whether your proxy itself can be detected; this one checks who sites think they are looking at — and how far that picture is from the one you expect to present.
personacheck.Note2: Start by choosing the country you want to be read as a local of.
personacheck.noProfile: This territory has no local profile to compare against.
personacheck.languageSingle: This country has a single primary language.
personacheck.languageMulti: This country has several languages — pick the one you want to present.
personacheck.timezoneMulti: This country spans several time zones — pick the one you want to present.

grade.A: 🎉 You look every bit like a local of {country}
grade.B: 😊 You look somewhat like a local of {country}
grade.C: 🤔 You don't quite look like a local of {country}
grade.D: 😅 You don't look like a local of {country}

gradeNote.A: Every signal we can read agrees with the persona you chose.
gradeNote.B: The persona mostly holds, but a few signals point elsewhere.
gradeNote.C: Several signals disagree with the persona, or with each other — the results below show which.
gradeNote.D: Most signals point somewhere other than this persona.
gradeNote.unknown: Run the underlying tests first — there is too little to go on.

report.nothingActionable: Nothing to fix — every measurable signal fits the persona.

verdict.unnatural: Internally inconsistent — two signals that should agree tell different stories, which draws more attention than a plain mismatch.

ip-country.title: IP country
ip-country.fix: Part of your exits land outside the target country — with several proxy exits, different cards genuinely show different countries, and any one exit is what some site will see. The fractions above say how many exits agree. Route everything through nodes in the target country; if a single source disagrees about one IP, that node may just be mislabelled in its database, which is not fixable from your side.
ip-country.what: Which country the IP lookup cards on the home page place your exit address in — every source is read, and every exit has to sit in the target country.

webrtc-leak.title: WebRTC exposure
webrtc-leak.fix: Block WebRTC, or use a setup where it can only ever see the proxy address. The cost is real: video calls and voice conferencing stop working. A browser extension that filters WebRTC is gentler than disabling it outright, but the extension itself leaves traces of its own.
webrtc-leak.what: Whether WebRTC hands out an address from a different country than your persona.

dns-resolver-country.title: DNS resolver country
dns-resolver-country.fix: Use a resolver in the target country, or let the proxy handle DNS resolution. Note that a public resolver like 1.1.1.1 will not expose your location, but it will not support your persona either — it is equally neutral for every country.
dns-resolver-country.what: Which country the DNS resolvers answering for you sit in.

asn-type.title: Address type
asn-type.fix: A datacenter range is the single loudest "this is a proxy" signal an address carries. A residential exit fixes it outright, but costs considerably more and varies a lot in quality.
asn-type.what: Whether your address belongs to a residential ISP or a datacenter range.

timezone-vs-persona.title: Time zone vs persona
timezone-vs-persona.fix: Change the time zone at the operating-system level — that way every browser API stays consistent with itself. Extensions that override the time zone often change only part of it, creating the contradictions flagged under the coherence checks, which is worse than not changing it at all.
timezone-vs-persona.what: Whether your browser's time zone is the one a local would have.

language-match.title: Browser language
language-match.fix: Change the language in your system or browser settings rather than rewriting a single HTTP header. The order matters too: sites read the whole list, and a local would rarely lead with a foreign language.
language-match.what: Whether the language your browser leads with is one a local would use.

script-fonts.title: Writing-system fonts
script-fonts.fix: A machine set up for this locale ships that writing system's fonts. Installing them by hand is possible but rarely worth it: it changes one signal while the rest of the system stays in its original language, which usually creates more contradictions than it resolves. If this needs to hold up, the system language itself is the thing to change.
script-fonts.what: Whether fonts for this country's writing system are installed on the machine.

speech-voices.title: Speech synthesis voices
speech-voices.fix: Text-to-speech packs follow the language your OS was installed with, and essentially no proxy or spoofing extension touches them. Adding a voice pack for the target language is a real fix, with the same caveat as fonts: one changed signal inside an otherwise unchanged system reads as deliberate.
speech-voices.what: Which languages the text-to-speech packs on your system cover.

keyboard-layout.title: Keyboard layout
keyboard-layout.fix: Your physical keyboard layout is not what is typical for the target country. Only Chromium browsers expose this, so it is a narrower signal than the others — but wherever it is readable, it is hard to fake without changing the actual keyboard.
keyboard-layout.what: Which physical keyboard layout your machine reports.

edge-geo-consensus.title: Edge geolocation
edge-geo-consensus.fix: Cloudflare's own reading of your exit address disagrees with the target country. When this and the IP lookup contradict each other, the address is more likely mislabelled in one database than actually moving — but every site behind Cloudflare sees this verdict, not the other one.
edge-geo-consensus.what: Cloudflare's own reading of your exit address, formed independently of the databases above.

accept-language-header.title: Language header vs script
accept-language-header.fix: The Accept-Language header your browser sends on the wire does not match what navigator.languages reports to scripts. Almost nothing produces this except an extension that rewrote one and left the other. Change the language in your browser or system settings instead — that moves both at once.
accept-language-header.what: Whether the language header sent on the wire matches what scripts are told. Deliberately independent of the target country: a pass only says your two language channels agree — whether the language itself fits is the Browser language check's job. Half-applied language spoofs fail exactly here.

ip-timezone-vs-browser.title: IP time zone vs browser
ip-timezone-vs-browser.fix: The time zone of your exit IP and the one your browser reports are different places. This holds whichever country you are aiming for: a real machine sits somewhere, and both should say the same somewhere. Usually it means the proxy moved your address but not your system clock.
ip-timezone-vs-browser.what: Whether the time zone of your IP and the one your browser reports agree.

gps-location.title: Device location (GPS)
gps-location.fix: Your device reports being physically in a different country than the one you are aiming for. No proxy touches this: any site that asks for your location gets the real answer, and browser extensions that fake it typically leave the accuracy and timing patterns intact. The realistic options are to deny location permission for sites that ask, or to accept that this one will not hold up.
gps-location.what: Which country your device reports being physically in.

payment-region.title: Card issuer country
payment-region.fix: Your card was issued in a different country than the one you are presenting as. Merchants see the issuing country before almost anything else, and payment risk systems weigh it heavily against the address and IP. There is no browser-side fix for this — it is a property of the card itself.
payment-region.what: Which country issued the card behind the prefix you entered.

intl-number-format.title: Number format
intl-number-format.what: How your browser groups digits and marks decimals.
intl-number-format.fix: Your browser groups numbers the way its own region does, not the way the target country does. This is separate from the language: a machine can carry the right language tag while its region still says elsewhere. Change the region — not just the language — in your system settings: Region on Windows, Language & Region on macOS.

intl-date-format.title: Date format
intl-date-format.what: The order and separators your browser uses when writing a date.
intl-date-format.fix: Your browser writes dates in a different order or with different separators than a local would. Like the number format, this follows the system region rather than the language, and changing the region is what moves it.

intl-hour-cycle.title: Clock format
intl-hour-cycle.what: Whether your browser presents a 12-hour or 24-hour clock — the convention sites see when they format times.
intl-hour-cycle.fix: The clock format follows the browser's language, not the system's 24-hour toggle — most browsers ignore that switch entirely (Safari is the main exception). To present the target country's convention, switch the browser's language or region to a locale of that country.

timezone-authenticity.title: Time zone authenticity
timezone-authenticity.what: Whether the time zone your browser reports is the machine's real one.
timezone-authenticity.fix: The zone your browser reports is not the one the machine actually runs on: Intl and Date disagree, or past dates do not follow that zone's daylight-saving rules. This matters because it means the timezone check above passed on a value that is not real — a site reading the clock directly sees through it. Set the zone in your operating system rather than with an extension, and both the current offset and the historical rules move together.

whois.Title: Whois Search
whois.Note: Whois search is a service used to retrieve domain registration information. By entering a domain name or IP address, you can retrieve information such as the domain's registration details, registrar, registration date, expiration date, and more. The Whois information for IP addresses and domain names may have different fields. Additionally, some less common top-level domains (TLDs) may not have available information for Whois queries.

whois.Note3: Whois information contains various types of fields. The following is the raw text information
whois.reservedIP: Private or reserved IP addresses have no public registry record, so there is nothing to look up.
whois.noData: No Whois or RDAP data is published for this query. Some top-level domains do not offer a public lookup service.
whois.fetchError: Unable to fetch query results or query results are empty

enhanceddnsleaktest.Title: In-depth DNS Leak Test
enhanceddnsleaktest.Note: The homepage DNS leak test already gave you a rough idea of whether you're leaking and where your DNS traffic exits. This deeper test adds more dimensions: it captures more of your resolver exit IPs, checks whether any of them forwards a prefix of your real IP upstream via ECS, and checks whether they support DNSSEC — so you come away with a more complete picture of your DNS chain's security posture.
enhanceddnsleaktest.Note2: Click Run to start. The test usually completes within a few seconds. We fire several DNS probes in the background and let our authoritative DNS server capture the recursive resolver exit IPs you're actually using — a typical run captures 20–40 records. If no resolvers show up at all, your browser's DNS cache probably absorbed the requests; just wait a moment and try again.
enhanceddnsleaktest.Note3: Since this is an in-depth test, you'll run into some specialized concepts on this page (ECS, DNSSEC, etc.). No worries — after running the test, check the "Field reference" at the bottom of the page for a short explanation of each column.
enhanceddnsleaktest.FetchError: Failed to fetch DNS leak test results. Please try again later.
enhanceddnsleaktest.Empty: No DNS resolvers were captured for this session. This usually means the browser DNS cache absorbed the request — try again in a moment.

Flow.Waiting: Waiting for recursive DNS to reach our name server (usually 1–3 s).

Summary.DnssecGood: DNSSEC-aware — every resolver requested signatures and none of them skipped validation.
Summary.DnssecNoDo: Weak — at least one resolver did not request DNSSEC signatures.
Summary.DnssecCdSet: Suspicious — at least one resolver asked to skip DNSSEC validation.

Legend.Title: Field reference
Legend.ResolverIP: The egress IP of the recursive DNS resolver that actually reached our authoritative name server. If you use a VPN, compare its ASN with the ASN of your VPN exit — a mismatch means your DNS queries are bypassing the VPN tunnel (i.e., leaking).
Legend.QueryType: The record type the resolver asked for on behalf of your browser (A, AAAA, HTTPS, etc.). Browsers typically fire A and AAAA queries together.
Legend.Transport: DNS defaults to UDP. TCP usually means the response was large — and responses tend to be large because they carry DNSSEC records.
Legend.ECS: EDNS Client Subnet — some recursive resolvers attach a prefix of your real IP (typically IPv4 /24 or IPv6 /48) when forwarding queries to upstream authoritative servers. That means a segment of your IP becomes known to servers along the DNS chain, which can be used for CDN geo-routing but also chips away at your anonymity.
Legend.DO: DNSSEC OK — a check means the recursive resolver actively requested DNSSEC signatures on this query, so the chain carries cryptographic verification; a cross means the query went out without signatures, so a tampered response on the wire could go undetected.
Legend.CD: Checking Disabled — a check means the caller did not ask to skip DNSSEC validation, so the recursive resolver performs normal signature verification; a cross means the caller explicitly asked to skip validation and will accept responses even when signatures don't match. Normally this should be a check; if you see a cross, it's usually because of a debugging tool or a client's security-downgrade behavior, and in rare cases a signal of man-in-the-middle tampering on the path.

dnsresolver.Title: DNS Resolution
dnsresolver.Note: Resolve one domain against well-known public DNS providers around the world at the same time — over both classic DNS and DNS-over-HTTPS — and compare what each one answers. When the answers differ between providers or regions, it usually means a CDN is steering traffic to a nearby node, a cache somewhere is stale, or the record is being filtered or redirected along the way. Pick a record type, enter a domain or URL, and run the query: each row shows which country the resolver sits in, and the table can be filtered by region.
dnsresolver.Note2: Please enter a URL or domain name to start resolution:

ruletest.Title: Rule Test
ruletest.Name: Test
ruletest.Note: Rule test is used to determine if the proxy software's domain-based rules are set correctly. Before conducting the test, you need to refer to the card below and set different domain-based routing rules for the 8 different URLs of IPCheck.ing in your proxy software. Usually, the rule settings may use a format like: DOMAIN, ptest-3.ipcheck.ing, POLICY. The specific format may vary depending on the proxy software you are using.

report.Title: Diagnostic Report
report.Note: Bundle your completed test results into one report and share it with a friend or an AI assistant for network diagnosis. Nothing leaves this device until you copy, download or create a link.
report.NoSelection: Select at least one test first.
report.CreateFailed: Creating the share link failed, please try again later.

ai.Heading: MyIP Network Diagnostic Report
ai.Intro: This report was generated by MyIP ({origin}) at {time} from network tests run in the user's browser. Field names are stable schema identifiers; all latency values are in milliseconds.
ai.Masked: Note: IP addresses are partially masked for privacy (IPv4: last octet, IPv6: interface half, shown as "x").
ai.Instruction: Based on the data above, analyze the health of this network. Point out anomalies (DNS leaks, WebRTC exposure, proxy/VPN traits, packet loss, high latency, routing issues) and give concrete troubleshooting suggestions.

Sections.ipinfo: Public IP addresses as seen by multiple independent sources (sources may disagree when a proxy or split routing is involved).
Sections.connectivity: Browser reachability probes against well-known websites; timeMs is the displayed round-trip, minTimeMs the best of repeated rounds.
Sections.webrtc: IPs exposed through WebRTC STUN — if these differ from the main public IP, the real address may be leaking past a proxy/VPN.
Sections.dnsleak: Egress IPs of the DNS resolvers that actually answered the browser's lookups — resolvers not belonging to the user's ISP/VPN provider indicate a DNS leak.
Sections.speedtest: Bandwidth, latency and loaded latency (bufferbloat) measured against Cloudflare; scores rate streaming/gaming/RTC experience, higher is better.
Sections.pingtest: ICMP ping statistics toward the user's IP from Globalping probes around the world.
Sections.mtrtest: Per-hop MTR traceroutes toward the user's IP from probes around the world; loss at intermediate hops can be mere ICMP rate-limiting, sustained loss from one hop onward indicates a real problem.
Sections.ruletest: Egress IPs observed when fetching 8 test endpoints — more than one unique IP means traffic is split across different routes (e.g. proxy rules).
Sections.browserinfo: Browser, OS and display environment of the tested device.
Sections.invisibility: Proxy/VPN detection scores (0-100, higher = more likely detected) with the individual detection signals that flagged.
Sections.enhanceddnsleak: Resolver-level DNS capture: every resolver IP that queried the test domain, with transport, ECS exposure and DNSSEC flags (do/cd).
Sections.persona: How closely the browser matches a local resident of the chosen country: an overall grade plus each check's verdict. Verdicts only — the underlying values are deliberately not stored in a shared report.

serviceStatus.Title: Service Status
serviceStatus.Note: When a service won't open, it might not be your problem — the service itself could be down. Currently, people are using a lot of AI products, and when the AI product doesn't reply, they don't know if it's their problem or the service's problem. This section shows the live availability of well-known AI services; expand a card to see each sub-service's status and recent incidents.

connectivity.Title: Network Connectivity
connectivity.Note: This test checks your connectivity to a website. The higher the latency, the slower your connection to that site. You can import or add other websites you frequently use to the test list for quick testing.

addCustom.Hint: We test by loading the site's favicon over HTTPS. Some sites may not be reachable this way. Custom tests are saved locally in your browser.
addCustom.ProbeBlockedNote: Some sites' security policies block cross-origin probes — they can show as unreachable even though they open fine.

webrtc.Title: WebRTC Leak Test
webrtc.Name: WebRTC Connection
webrtc.Note: When the browser obtains network addresses through WebRTC, it may bypass your VPN or proxy and expose your real IP to websites. This test checks which IP is exposed when you connect over WebRTC; if the returned IP address or region is not what you expect, there may be a risk of WebRTC leaks and you may need to adjust your proxy settings. Besides the IP used for WebRTC connections, we also detect your NAT type.

dnsleaktest.Name: DNS Endpoint Test
dnsleaktest.Title: DNS Leak Test
dnsleaktest.Note: Even while you are using a VPN or proxy, DNS queries may still be sent over your local network, exposing the domains of the sites you visit. ISPs, firewalls, public Wi-Fi providers and others along the path can intercept them and learn which sites you are visiting. This test visits a newly generated domain name to detect which region your DNS queries go through; if the returned region differs from the region of the VPN/proxy you are using, there may be a risk of DNS leaks.

speedtest.Title: Speed Test
speedtest.Note: The speed test will be conducted using Cloudflare's edge network. You can choose the packet size for download and upload according to your needs. During the test, packets will be uploaded and downloaded 4 times — please be mindful of data usage. Since Cloudflare does not deploy edge nodes in every country worldwide, the results are for reference only; actual speeds may be faster.
speedtest.score: Based on the speed test, got the following quality scores:
speedtest.connectionFrom: Finished speed test from your machine, IP:

pingtest.Title: Global Latency Test
pingtest.Note: Ping test is a network tool used to measure the round-trip time of data packets between two endpoints (servers). It is a key metric for evaluating network performance.
pingtest.Note2: In the test below, IPCheck.ing uses Globalping's worldwide probes to send small packets of data from servers around the world to your IP address, measuring the time it takes for these packets to travel from the server to your device and back. Through these Ping tests from different geographical locations, you can gain a comprehensive view of the speed and stability of your device's connection to the global network.
pingtest.Note3: Please select your IP address for testing.
pingtest.Error: Test failed, it looks like your IP is not allowed to perform Ping test.

mtrtest.Title: MTR Test
mtrtest.Note: The MTR (My Traceroute) test uses Globalping's worldwide probes to perform detailed route tracing of your IP address from servers located in different continents and regions around the world. MTR combines the functionality of traditional traceroute and ping commands to diagnose the quality and performance of network connections in real-time.
mtrtest.Note2: This process covers the complete path from various geographical locations to your network environment, providing information on latency and packet loss for each hop. Whether it's congestion in the routing path, latency issues at a specific node, or packet loss during transmission, the MTR test provides critical diagnostic information.

about.Title: About
project: IPCheck.ing is a free all-in-one IP toolbox that helps you check your own IP information, test website availability, examine DNS exit information, and run speed tests, global latency tests, MTR tests and more.
This is an open-source project — click the GitHub icon at the bottom of the page to browse the source code.

If you are unsure how a feature works, open the "Help Center" link at the bottom of the page. The documentation is thorough: beyond describing each feature, it also explains networking concepts and how to troubleshoot network problems.
If you would like to take part in the open-source project, click the "Contribute Code" button at the bottom of the page to see how.
founder: This started out as a side project for Jason Ng (阿禅) to learn Vue.js and how to write code with AI. As it collected more and more stars on GitHub, he refactored it heavily and added many genuinely useful features. We hope you enjoy it.
He is not a professional programmer. Most of the time he works as a product manager, a blogger, a motorcycle rider and a geek — but he loves coding, open source and sharing.
You can find a more detailed introduction about him at the links below:
contact: If you run into trouble using IPCheck.ing or deploying the MyIP project, head to the "Help Center" first. If you cannot find the answer there and are stuck, open an issue on GitHub or reach us by email.
And if you hit a bug and enjoy coding (or coding with AI), you are very welcome to send us a PR with your fix.
